body.en:
Crafting our own desires in everyday life is of critical importance. This is not a philosophical aside. It is an operational matter with measurable consequences.

In Zen meditation practice there is a figure called the hungry ghost — a being with a vast empty belly and a tiny mouth, always consuming, never satisfied. The hungry ghost is not a metaphor for bad people. It is a description of a specific condition: when desire and immediate gratification collapse human temporality, the future becomes a projection of the past. The person is not choosing. They are repeating.

David Foster Wallace gave this condition a contemporary name: the age of entertainment. Not entertainment as rest, but entertainment as a technology that organizes attention, rhythm, expectation, and relief into a loop. The experience of dwelling in a present eaten by craving and pulled by immediate satisfaction. He saw it in the 1990s. The infrastructure has since been refined considerably.

Cambridge Analytica demonstrated that a couple of dozen likes are enough to know a person better than they know themselves — and to influence their voting preferences using a team of engineers tracking decisions along the traceable metadata of social networks. Mark Zuckerberg engineered the business at global scale, targeting adolescents. Yuval Noah Harari calls the result "humans that have been hacked." Cult organizations build institutional order using desire as the access hook. The mechanism varies. The structural pattern is consistent: gain access to the machinery of wanting, and conduct follows.

Desires do not carry primordial meaning. They are genetically embodied, and shaped by repetition, trauma, inculcation — or by self-refinement and mastery. Yuja Wang's desire for piano was composed through wonder, relational friction, and decades of disciplined practice. A cohort of Scottish youth acquired their desire for heroin through laced marijuana they never chose to consume. Same word — desire. Radically different genesis, radically different consequences.

Shaping our own desires is a fundamental aspect of adulthood. Buddha addressed it. Plato addressed it. Descartes discovered, late in life and through correspondence with Princess Elizabeth of Bohemia, that desire belongs to a domain knowable only through lived engagement and ordinary conversation — not through the method of clear and distinct ideas. Kierkegaard addressed it. Freud addressed it. Countless accounts across traditions of a contested territory. Source of excellence and self-destruction. Not a minor subject.

And yet.

When modern economic theory formalized desire into its foundational models, something specific happened. Menger, Jevons, and Walras — the marginalist revolution of the 1870s — grounded economic value in the relationship between an agent's need and a good's capacity to satisfy it. In doing so, they performed two operations.

First, they took desire out of its relational, temporal, and institutional context and placed it inside the individual mind as a given — a subjective assessment requiring no further examination. The question of how desires form, through what relationships, under what conditions, with what degree of the person's own participation — that question fell outside the model.

Second, they reversed the direction of value. In classical economics, value flows forward from production — labor creates what was not there before. In the marginalist model, value flows backward from consumption — the agent's need assigns value to everything upstream. Labor becomes an instrument. The commons — shared knowledge, shared resources, shared institutional infrastructure — becomes invisible until it is scarce enough to price.

The consequences are traceable. A framework that takes desires as given data cannot distinguish between a desire that builds capacity and one that depletes it. It cannot distinguish Yuja Wang returning to the piano from a teenager returning to a feed engineered for compulsive engagement. Both register as preferences being satisfied. Both count as value being created.

A framework that locates all value in the consuming agent's need has no variable for the relational field in which desire actually forms — the family, the community, the institutional conditions that make genuine desire-formation possible. When those conditions degrade, the degradation does not register as a problem in the model. It registers as more preferences being satisfied.

A framework that classifies every household purchase as consumption — expensed immediately, treated as used up — cannot see the household as what it is: a going concern, one of the oldest forms of economic composition, producing persons capable of relationship, language, trust, and the kind of engagement from which real desire can emerge.

These are not accusations. They are specifications of what the model does not contain and the consequences that follow from each omission.

Here is the opportunity.

Everything the marginalist model leaves out is still operating. Desires still form relationally. The commons still sustains economic life. Labor still creates what was not there before. Families still produce persons. Citizens still compose institutional order. The going concern — people committing to shared undertaking — is still the primary unit of economic life.

These are not lost. They are unmodeled. And what is unmodeled can be modeled. What is unaccounted for can be accounted for. What has been left out of the equations can be put back in.

A framework that includes the genesis of desire — the process by which needs are articulated in conversation, in committed engagement with others — can distinguish between desires that compose and desires that deplete. That distinction has direct consequences for service design, product architecture, institutional policy, and investment.

A framework that includes modes of existence — the worker, the family, the commoner, the artisan, the citizen — as distinct ways of being in economic life, each with its own conditions of success and failure, can design services that sustain those modes rather than subordinating all of them to a single empty category.

A framework that includes the relational field — the I-We from which economic activity actually emerges — can see the going concern as the primary institutional arrangement and design for its durability rather than optimizing for transactions at the point of exchange.

The waste is identifiable: value destroyed when desires are treated at face value and the conditions for genuine desire-formation are degraded without detection. The value is recoverable: services, institutions, and designs that account for how desires actually form, what sustains them, and what distinguishes composition from depletion.

This is what Desires as Economic Foundation is attempting to grasp — and to incorporate into sustainable service design. The machinery of wanting is not going away. The question is whether we design with an accurate model of how it works, or continue operating with equations that leave out the forces that determine whether the circuit produces light or heat.

The forces are there. The wiring is traceable. The opportunity is to include what has been left out — and to build services that generate value for all relevant stakeholders by working with the actual structure of desire rather than the formalized remainder.
